correctness.rationale: The digit-sum identity holds without carries for all j because 0<R+jd<b; simultaneous Fermat congruences force b^(1+tL)=b mod every prime divisor of the corresponding digit sum, including primes dividing b. A common divisor would contradict gcd(b−1,H)=1. For upper sharpness any p-term step-d run has one p-multiple with digit sum also a p-multiple. CRT conditions are consistent since gcd(Q,2p)=1 and give precise positive natural density. A self-contained standard-library checker confirms 236 structured and 741 sieve parameter cases, six full large-integer constructions and a literal b=41 example; the proof, not finite testing, establishes universality.

originality.rationale: The full publicly accessible arXiv:2308.05228v1 establishes the p−1 obstruction, d=1 and d=2 sharpness, and an existence result allowing d to vary, then explicitly conjectures sharpness for arbitrary even d. The positive-density-base theorem for every d>=4 and corresponding explicit witnesses are not implied by these statements. Full text of a distinct 2023 Niven-divisibility paper also does not cover anti-Niven coprimality. Actual semantic mathematical-result and literature searches did not identify a covering claim. Later journal text is an explicitly retained originality risk.
residual_risks: A stronger theorem could appear in unindexed or inaccessible literature, including the later 2026 journal text of the same source.
An implicit corollary of published work using the same elementary construction is possible; the absence of search matches does not prove global uniqueness.

value.rationale: The theorem makes uniform quantified progress on an explicitly proposed even-step anti-Niven sharpness conjecture, for every even d>=4 and every eligible obstruction prime p, by proving exact maximality for a computable positive-density family of bases. The simultaneous-digit-sum CRT/Fermat mechanism supplies explicit infinite families and is broader than an isolated example or a routine finite table. It intentionally does not claim all bases or density of starting points.
